title: B-Trees and LSM Trees
description: Understand how databases store data on disk — B-trees for read-heavy workloads and LSM trees for write-heavy workloads.

segments.text: Welcome to expert territory. Today we're going inside the database engine itself. How does a database actually store and retrieve data from disk? The answer is two competing data structures: B-trees and LSM trees.

Disk reads are measured in blocks — typically four kilobytes each. Reading one byte costs the same as reading four thousand. So the key insight: minimize the number of disk reads per query. Every data structure decision revolves around this.
A B-tree is a self-balancing tree where each node can hold hundreds of keys. High branching factor means a tree with millions of keys is only three or four levels deep. Each level is one disk read.

Looking up a key? Start at the root. Binary search within the node to find the right child pointer. Follow it. Repeat. Three levels deep means three disk reads for any key among millions. That's O(log n) — but with a massive branching factor.
segments.thought_prompt: If each node holds 500 keys, how many keys can a 3-level B-tree store?

segments.text: Insertions find the correct leaf node and add the key. If the leaf overflows, it splits into two nodes, pushing a key up to the parent. This splitting cascades upward if needed — that's how B-trees stay balanced automatically.
Now, LSM trees. Writes go to an in-memory sorted structure called a memtable — usually a red-black tree or skip list. This is blazing fast because it's all in RAM. No disk I/O on the write path.

When the memtable fills up, it's flushed to disk as an SSTable — a Sorted String Table. SSTables are immutable, sorted files. Reads must check the memtable first, then search through SSTables on disk. More SSTables means slower reads.

To keep reads fast, LSM trees run compaction — merging multiple SSTables into fewer, larger ones while removing deleted and overwritten entries. It's like merge sort on disk. But compaction uses CPU and disk I/O in the background.
segments.thought_prompt: What happens to read latency if compaction falls behind and SSTables pile up?

segments.text: B-trees excel at reads — O(log n) with minimal disk seeks. LSM trees excel at writes — sequential I/O, no random writes. B-trees have write amplification from in-place updates. LSM trees have read and space amplification from multiple SSTables.

PostgreSQL and MySQL use B-trees. Cassandra, RocksDB, and LevelDB use LSM trees. Some databases like TiDB use both — B-tree indexes on top of an LSM storage engine. Choose based on your read/write ratio.

B-trees minimize disk reads with high branching factor. LSM trees minimize disk writes with sequential I/O and compaction. Neither is universally better — it depends on your workload. That's the fundamental trade-off of database storage engines.
